newsitem.title: USA: NY Times report on Holocaust funds disputed.
newsitem.headline: NY Times report on Holocaust funds disputed.

text.p: The New York Times said on Wednesday Swiss banks recently found hundreds of accounts that might belong to Holocaust victims, but the head of an investigative panel and a Swiss bank group denied the report.

The newspaper also said banks had found 15,000 to 20,000 other accounts whose origins could not be determined. It said the disclosures were made last week in Jerusalem and Bern to an independent commission headed by Paul Volcker, the former head of the U.S. Federal Reserve.

The reports could raise new questions about whether the banks sought to hide the accounts to avoid turning them over to the heirs of the Holocaust victims. However, Volcker, in an interview with Reuters, denied that information on newly found accounts had been turned over to his panel.
A spokesman for the Swiss Bankers Association said the story of recently discovered accounts of Holocaust victims had been "taken from thin air."

Volcker said Swiss banks did not present evidence at the Jerusalem and Bern hearings. "This idea that they whispered in our ear in Bern or Jerusalem that they had made some new discoveries is not right," he said.
The Washington-datelined story "implies that another deluge of money had been found," he said. "I'd be delighted if another deluge had been found but there has been none at this point."

His panel, empowered by Swiss banks to waive bank rules in order to scrutinise wartime records, is about to start a series of "pilot audits" of accounts opened between 1933 and 1945, when Nazis were in power in Germany. The audits are designed to determine how many accounts contain deposits placed in Switzerland by Jews or others to prevent their money from falling into Nazi hands.

The Times said that, according to people familiar with meetings between the bankers and Volcker's commission, the banks have found more than 1,000 accounts opened in the names of non-Swiss during the Second World War era. The accounts hold more than $40 million.
It added that the discovery of the new accounts came from banks that had not completed full surveys of accounts.

Last Thursday, a source close to the Volcker commission told Reuters the number of unclaimed Holocaust-era Jewish accounts in Swiss banks may be "dramatically higher" than the figure of 774 that Swiss bankers said they found in 1995.

The Swiss Bankers Association said two years ago that the 774 accounts contained about $32 million in unclaimed funds. In Zurich, association spokesman Heinrich Schneider said no new accounts opened by possible Holocaust victims had turned up since the middle of 1996.

"There is no basis for this story that I can see and therefore it seems to be taken from thin air," Schneider told Reuters. He said the numbers remained the same as those made public by the banks last year.

The Times said there were another 15,000 to 20,000 dormant accounts that were opened by Swiss nationals during the war years. In response to questions, the Swiss Bankers Association said in a statement late on Tuesday that the amounts in the accounts were small, the newspaper said.
The association promised that "the Volcker committee will fully examine whether dormant accounts opened by Swiss citizens prior to 1945 were opened for the benefit of Holocaust victims."
